title: Delhi High Court Blocks Vinesh Phogat From Asian Games Wrestling Trials
excerpt: India's three-time Olympian denied interim relief as WFI's revised eligibility rules and anti-doping charges keep her off the mat
body:
The Delhi High Court has declined to grant interim relief to wrestler Vinesh Phogat, effectively blocking her participation in the selection trials for the 2026 Asian Games. The ruling leaves the three-time Olympian's competitive future in limbo, with the court scheduling the next hearing for July 6 — well past the trial window.

Context & Background

Vinesh Phogat's career has been defined by extraordinary athletic achievement shadowed by institutional conflict. A member of India's most celebrated wrestling family — cousin to Geeta and Babita Phogat, the subjects of the Bollywood film Dangal — she won gold at the 2018 Asian Games and Commonwealth Games, becoming one of India's most decorated wrestlers.

Her trajectory shifted dramatically at the Paris 2024 Olympics, where she was disqualified before the gold medal bout for being 100 grams overweight — a decision that generated a global outcry and brought unprecedented attention to weight-cutting practices in combat sports. The episode left deep institutional scars: Phogat initially announced her retirement, then reversed course and began training for a comeback.

The Wrestling Federation of India (WFI), however, moved to exclude her. The federation issued a show cause notice citing alleged anti-doping rule violations, breaches of weight regulations, and indiscipline. More critically, WFI introduced revised selection criteria for the 2026 Asian Games trials, requiring participants to have won medals at either the 2025 Senior National Wrestling Championships, the 2026 Senior Federation Cup, or the Under-20 National Wrestling Championships. Having competed in none of these events during her period away from the mat, Phogat was rendered ineligible by design.

Current Developments

Phogat challenged the WFI's criteria in the Delhi High Court, arguing that the new rules were discriminatory and specifically crafted to exclude her. Her petition sought interim relief that would allow her to compete in the trials while the broader legal challenge was adjudicated.

The court, while issuing notice to the WFI, declined to grant immediate relief. The bench observed that balancing national sporting interests against individual athlete rights required careful consideration, and that the WFI should first resolve its show cause proceedings. The matter is now listed for July 6, after the court's summer vacation.

The practical effect is decisive: with the Asian Games trials scheduled before that date, Phogat cannot participate unless the WFI voluntarily reverses its position — a prospect that appears remote given the federation's public stance. The WFI has reportedly characterised the Paris 2024 disqualification as a "national embarrassment," language that suggests the dispute extends beyond procedural eligibility into institutional politics.

Diaspora Impact

The case has resonated strongly with the Indian diaspora, where Phogat became a household name during the Paris Olympics controversy. NRI communities, particularly in the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom, had rallied behind her during the 2023 wrestlers' protest against the previous WFI president and again during the Paris weight disqualification.

For diaspora audiences, the case highlights a recurring tension in Indian sport: the gap between world-class athletes and the governance structures meant to support them. Several overseas Indian sporting organisations have voiced support for Phogat on social media, calling for transparent selection processes.

The timing also matters. The 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, will feature a significant diaspora audience — both in person and via streaming — making the absence of India's most internationally recognised wrestler all the more conspicuous.

What's Next

The July 6 hearing will be pivotal. If the court finds the WFI's revised criteria to be arbitrary or discriminatory, it could order the federation to allow Phogat to compete in subsequent selection events. However, the Asian Games trials themselves may have concluded by then, leaving Phogat's 2026 participation effectively foreclosed regardless of the legal outcome.

Phogat's legal team has indicated she aims to compete at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics — a goal that requires both competitive readiness and institutional clearance. The Delhi HC proceedings will likely set a precedent for athlete-federation disputes in Indian sport, a domain where the balance of power has historically favoured governing bodies.

For now, one of India's most decorated combat athletes remains sidelined — not by injury or form, but by the machinery meant to field her.
